newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Dlr's ideal level hard to define - Camdessus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dlr's ideal level hard to define - Camdessus.

text.p: IMF head Michel Camdessus said on Friday it was not possible to measure the "orderly reversal" of the dollar, which was called for by the Group of Seven nations in 1995, to the nearest cent or French franc at a given moment.
Camdessus, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, said in an interview in French daily Le Monde the dollar, yen and European currencies were in a "zone of plausibility".

"Some will say the dollar has overshot the desirable level a little, notably vis-a-vis the yen," he was quoted as saying. "You cannot say, to the nearest cent or franc what is 'The' right level at a given time," he added.
Camdessus travels to Berlin on Saturday for the G7 weekend meeting.

Asked about the optimism on the economic outlook emerging from the Davos meeting of business leaders and politicians, Camdessus said: "There is a general optimism, with one exception -- Europe -- but it is not a self-satisfied optimism".

"This relatively reassuring situation in the world economy reflects healthy policies, generally applied with perseverance and continuity, not a windfall which could result from a wonderful movement in raw materials prices, and of favourable turns in exchange levels," he said.
He said the outlook for 1997 was good for world economies as a whole, with the exception of Europe, and that this could last for four or five years as long as policies were kept steady.
"We're staying within a growth zone which is at the level of the potential of economies and I do not perceive inflationary pressures anywhere in the large industrialised countries," he said.
"A culture of stability is developing, in the United States and in Europe, as we can see in extremely moderate wage behaviour. Therefore, I do not see why central banks would 'cry wolf'," he said.
Japan had been hard shaken by financial sector crisis, which would require that it consolidate "over a few years", he said.
This crisis resulted in it needing to make a huge budgetary growth stimulation effort to avoid recession.
"The yen should not continue to fall to an extent that would lead the central bank to raise interest rates because that would have the effect of putting the brakes on growth," he said.

Asked whether he saw the debate over Europe threatening the launch of the euro single currency, Camdessus said he believed that "public opinion now seems ripe to accept normal monetary discipline in all the countries which want a healthy currency".

"I don't believe there is such tension in Europe, and above all that it could derail the advance to the euro, on which I believe the potential for growth has not been fully sized up by the Europeans yet," he said.

Camdessus said he saw no reason why the emergence of the euro group would lead to a "battle of the (euro, dollar, yen currency) blocs". This danger would have been clear years ago if it were the case, he said.
